title: AI carrier negotiation: Get the right driver, faster
summary: AI carrier negotiation is how Curri finds a driver fast, sending offers to many drivers at once and locking one in automatically. See how Negotiator works.
body_markdown:
AI carrier negotiation is the process of a software agent sending, tracking, and closing delivery offers with several drivers or carriers at once, instead of working the phones one carrier at a time.[Negotiator](https://www.curri.com/ai) , one of Curri's Core Intelligence AI agents, runs this process end to end.


It sends an offer to a pool of drivers, watches the replies come in, tracks who's in and at what spot rate, and locks in a carrier for the job fast. For a branch manager, that means requesting a delivery and getting back a driver and a rate, without ever getting bogged down in the search happening behind it.


## What is AI carrier negotiation?


AI carrier negotiation means software works the phones instead of a person doing it one carrier at a time. The old way of finding a driver meant calling carrier after carrier, repeating the same pickup and delivery details, waiting on hold, and going with whoever said yes first, whether or not that was a fair rate.


Negotiator changes the order of operations. It sends the same job to a dozen drivers simultaneously and collects every reply as it comes in, then delivers one clear answer: who's in, and what it costs. That's a meaningful shift from how carrier management has worked for years, where finding capacity meant burning time before a single delivery even started moving.


## How does Negotiator find and book a driver?


Negotiator sends a delivery offer to multiple qualified drivers at the same time, then manages every reply as it lands. It doesn't wait for one driver to answer before trying the next. It runs the whole negotiation in parallel, the way a person could if they never got tired and never lost track of a text message.


As drivers respond, Negotiator tracks each one against the job: rate quoted, availability, and how quickly they answered. It locks in the carrier that clears the bar on price and timing, and it does all of this without a person managing a spreadsheet or a group text. The branch only sees the outcome: driver assigned, rate confirmed, job moving.


This runs the same way whether the load is a single jobsite delivery or a batch of orders going out that morning, which matters for distributors juggling[Hotshots](https://www.curri.com/hotshots) ,[Dedicated Routes](https://www.curri.com/dedicated) , and[LTL](https://www.curri.com/ltl) freight on the same day.


## What does driver sourcing look like once Negotiator takes over?


Before Negotiator, a rush order could take a while to get covered. It goes out to one carrier at a time, each round adding minutes before there's even an answer on whether the job is covered, until the third call finally lands a yes.


After Negotiator, that same rush order goes out to several drivers at once the moment it's entered, and a confirmed driver and rate come back faster than the old way could finish its first callback. The branch moves on to the next task, the next[hotshot delivery](https://www.curri.com/hotshots) that needs eyes on it, without waiting to hear whether this one's covered. That's the real change: driver sourcing stops being a bottleneck and starts keeping pace with the rest of the day.


## How is this different from a load board or a carrier module in a TMS?


A load board shows available capacity, but a person still has to post the job, field calls, and pick a winner by hand. Some enterprise freight platforms have started building AI into procurement too, but those tools are built for national freight contracts: quarterly bid cycles across full truckload, ocean, and air lanes at scale.


Negotiator solves a different problem: the one-off, same-day, needs-a-driver-now reality of a distributor branch. It's built for the branch that needs one reliable carrier for one jobsite delivery in the next hour, not a quarterly bid cycle across a national lane network. That's a smaller problem on paper, but it's the one that actually holds up a distributor's morning when it isn't solved fast.


## What does this mean for HVAC, plumbing, and building materials distributors?


Distributors in HVAC, plumbing, electrical, and building materials run on tight delivery windows, and a missing driver on a Tuesday morning can hold up a jobsite crew that's already on site waiting for parts. The old way of searching for a driver meant leaning on the same three carriers and hoping one would answer the phone. Negotiator fills that gap automatically instead.


It also plugs into the rest of how a distributor already delivers. A branch might run[Route Planner](https://www.curri.com/route-planner) for its own fleet's daily stops and turn to[LTL](https://www.curri.com/ltl) for palletized freight that doesn't need a dedicated truck. When overflow or urgent jobsite runs come up, Negotiator is what finds the driver behind the scenes. The overflow and urgent side is where rate volatility hits hardest:[hotshot delivery costs](https://www.curri.com/blog/hotshot-delivery-cost-factors-what-impacts-the-final-price) shift based on distance, load size, and urgency, and negotiating one call at a time leaves no easy way to know if the first yes is actually the best price. Negotiator answers that by working several drivers at once instead of settling for the first call that picks up, and every driver it books still shows up in the same[last-mile carrier tracking](https://www.curri.com/blog/curri-glossary-last-mile-carrier-tracking) a distributor already uses to keep branch managers and customers updated in real time.
